changes.after: The second is filtration depth. A transfer in $F^r\Bcal$ vanishes modulo $F^r\Bcal$. This membership gives a lower bound on its depth. changes.before: Every packet of $\Rcal$ lies in one product packet.  Summing the packets with the same pair of parents reconstructs that product packet.
changes.after:
Every packet of $\Rcal$ lies in one product packet. Multiplying $\sum_\gamma R_\gamma=I_X$ by $P_\alpha Q_\beta$ and using the parent identities gives
\[
P_\alpha Q_\beta
=\sum_{\substack{\gamma:\ P_\alpha R_\gamma=R_\gamma\\Q_\beta R_\gamma=R_\gamma}}R_\gamma.
\]
Thus the packets with the same pair of parents reconstruct the product packet. If that product packet is nonzero, the sum has a child, so the parent map onto the supported product family is surjective.

changes.before:
If $\OO$ is a complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$, the filtration
\[
F^L\Bcal=\pi^L\Bcal
\]
is the standard example.  Basic facts about completeness in this setting are reviewed in \cite{Serre1979}.
changes.after:
In the filtration topology, reduction to $\Bcal/F^L\Bcal$ is continuous when the quotient has the discrete topology. Its kernel $F^L\Bcal$ is therefore closed. In particular, a convergent sum of terms in $F^L\Bcal$ remains in that ideal.

If $\OO$ is a complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$ and $\Bcal$ is a separated and complete $\OO$ algebra for the filtration
\[
F^L\Bcal=\pi^L\Bcal,
\]
then this is a standard example. Finite matrix algebras over $\OO$ satisfy these conditions. Completeness of $\OO$ alone does not imply completeness of every $\OO$ algebra. Basic facts about completeness in this setting are reviewed in \cite{Serre1979}.
